title: Shakespeare meets Sasquatch as La Conner festivals combine
excerpt: LA CONNER — Gilkey Square in La Conner became the "court of Sir Sasquatchalot," with bards clad in doublets sharing the square with face-painted children hunting Bigfoot.
content:
LA CONNER — Gilkey Square in La Conner became the "court of Sir Sasquatchalot," with bards clad in doublets sharing the square with face-painted children hunting Bigfoot.

For the first time, La Conner Thrives' Fables Faire ran in tandem with the Friends of Bigfoot Fun Fest organized by Mystic Art Supply.

"I thought, 'Why not? Fables, myths legends,'" said Julie Smith, La Conner Thrives' creative director.

The Gilkey Square main stage hosted the Washington Shakespearean Festival's events, which included music, belly dancing, combat demonstrations, fire dancing and medieval history.

Along First Street — at the event's entrance and trolley stop — a Bigfoot performer greeted everyone coming in.

Those attending dressed in everything from armor to homemade jester costumes.

This was the Fables Faire's second year, and Bigfoot Fest's third.

"I wanted an event to happen in September because our tourism really dives after school gets back into session," said Danielle Dunlap, owner of Mystic Art Supply and Bigfoot Fest organizer. "And I like Bigfoot. It seemed like something that fit very well into Skagit County."

Smith and Dunlap said the pairing drew hundreds of people, a sharp increase over the previous turnouts for the two events.

"This is three to four times the turnout we were expecting from last year's numbers," Dunlap said.

The event marked the first big test of the the trolley La Conner Thrives acquired just before the Fourth of July.

The Fables Faire had events all over La Conner happening throughout the day, and the Bigfoot Fest had a scavenger hunt at local businesses.

The trolley took people between the locations, and offered shuttle service from the parking lots on either end of town.

"All the businesses can be included if they want to be," Dunlap said.

The Washington Shakespeare Festival, which has toured the Pacific Northwest in one form or another for about 40 years, hosts everything from school presentations to weekendlong Renaissance faires, with a unique approach to Shakespeare's work.

"When I'm doing a Shakespeare scene, I'm not going to be ignoring you. I'm going to be involving you, I'm going to be talking to you," said Shakespearean Festival Managing Director GregRobin Smith. "That's the type of thing we like doing here."

The Washington Shakespearean Festival also hosts its own Renaissance faire once a year at the Skagit County Fairgrounds.

"We're going to be there the second weekend of June, from now until the ending of the world," Smith said.
